content: Retained placenta occurs in 0.5% to 3% of women after delivery and can lead to significant complications if not treated. Nitroglycerin (NTG), either used alone or in combination with uterotonics, has been proposed as a potential treatment to reduce the need for manual removal of the placenta under anesthesia. The objective of this study was to assess the benefits and risks of NTG as a tocolytic agent, either alone or alongside uterotonics, in managing retained placenta. The researchers conducted a systematic search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group’s Trials Register, reviewed reference lists of relevant studies, and consulted experts in the field. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared NTG, either alone or with uterotonics, to no intervention or other treatments in women with retained placenta following vaginal delivery. Only trials involving hemodynamically stable women whose placenta had not been delivered within at least 15 minutes after childbirth were included. Three RCTs involving a total of 175 women met the inclusion criteria. All three trials compared NTG alone to a placebo. The detachment status of the retained placenta was not specified in any of the studies. Two of the trials were judged to have a low risk of bias, while the third trial had a high risk of bias due to incomplete outcome data and selective reporting. The trials collectively reported seven of the 23 pre-specified outcomes for the review. The primary outcome, the need for manual removal of the placenta, was reported in all three studies. There was no significant difference between NTG and placebo in reducing the need for manual removal (average risk ratio [RR] 0.83, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.47 to 1.46; 175 women; I² = 81%). A random-effects model was used due to substantial heterogeneity in the analysis. Similarly, there were no differences between NTG and placebo in the risk of severe postpartum hemorrhage (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.39; 150 women; two studies; I² = 0%). Blood transfusion was reported in only one study involving 40 women, and no difference was observed between the groups (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.07 to 14.90; 40 women; I² = 0%). Mean blood loss, reported in all three studies, also showed no significant differences between NTG and placebo (mean difference [MD] -115.31 mL, 95% CI -306.25 to 75.63; 169 women; I² = 83%). NTG administration did not result in an increased incidence of headaches (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.47; 174 women; three studies; I² = 0%). However, NTG was associated with a mild but statistically significant decrease in systolic and diastolic blood pressure and an increase in pulse rate. Specifically, systolic blood pressure decreased by an average of 3.75 mmHg (MD -3.75, 95% CI -7.47 to -0.03), and pulse rate increased by an average of 6 beats per minute (MD 6.00, 95% CI 3.07 to 8.93). These hemodynamic effects were reported in only one study involving 24 participants. Maternal mortality and the use of additional therapeutic uterotonics were not reported in any of the included studies. In conclusion, the available evidence suggests that NTG alone does not reduce the need for manual removal of the placenta in cases of retained placenta. It also does not increase the risk of severe postpartum hemorrhage or the need for blood transfusion. Hemodynamically, NTG has a mild but significant effect on blood pressure and pulse rate.
